title: LLM-Enhanced Resilient UAV Swarm Operations in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks (IEEE TVT, submitted 2026)
reasoning_topology: Single supervisory LLM at swarm level consuming telemetry; not one LLM per vehicle; no multi-LLM debate.
embodiment: UAV/vehicle sim with dynamics+communication model (Swarm Squad platform, 3D voxel-grid environment, EW scenarios).
byzantine_model: none — no adversary modeled at reasoning layer; LLM assumed non-malicious, may be delayed/unavailable but not deceptive/adversarial.
aggregation_mechanism: Severity-dependent override/blending between single LLM output and deterministic baseline controller; not peer-to-peer aggregation.
graph_condition: not analyzed — time-varying directed comm graph G(t) defined, but no robustness (e.g., r-robust) condition analyzed.
actuation_gate: yes — severity-dependent override rule fuses LLM escape guidance with default controller; deterministic tangent-based fallback used when LLM unavailable/delayed.
message_format: structured/compact schema: swarm telemetry state summaries in, structured escape guidance out via MCP-inspired typed interface.
bandwidth_accounted: no — no token/bit or communication-cost metric reported for LLM queries.
contested_channel: yes — dominant-LoS distance-based link degradation plus multiplicative jamming-zone degradation factor (Dfinal) modeled explicitly.
determinism_evaluated: no — no repeatability/consistency-across-seeds analysis of LLM outputs reported in text.
evaluation_setup: Six 3D planners (A*, Theta*, Dijkstra, BFS, GBFS, Bidirectional A*) compared across 30 randomized EW/jamming scenarios per algorithm in Swarm Squad sim.
key_claim: A* with LLM assistance reduces mission completion time by 10.5% and path length by 11.6% while maintaining high communication quality.
does_not_do: The paper uses one centralized supervisory LLM, not one LLM per physical vehicle, so it has no receiver-side cross-agent Byzantine filtering, quorum voting, or collusion-resistant aggregation among multiple LLM instances. It also does not model an adversarial or hallucinating LLM, define a fault bound, or evaluate output determinism/repeatability, though it does gate LLM output through a severity-dependent override against a deterministic fallback controller.

title: LLM-Assisted Multi-Agent Transportation Systems Under Communication Attacks: A Survey (2026)
reasoning_topology: varies by architecture surveyed: centralized single coordinator, decentralized one-LLM-per-vehicle, hierarchical multi-tier, or shared-memory pool — paper compares these as taxonomy, not a proposed single system
embodiment: none built; discusses UAV/CAV/truck-platoon deployments and cites frameworks (SMART-LLM, COHERENT, AgentsCoDriver, LLM2Swarm) that use simulated robots/vehicles
byzantine_model: discusses prompt-tampering insider, compromised/malicious planner messages, shared-memory poisoning, and Sybil/phantom identities; treated qualitatively as attack classes, not formalized as a solved adversary model
aggregation_mechanism: surveys Byzantine consensus, robust aggregation, and trust-aware aggregation as a defense category (Sec IV-B) but does not implement or specify a concrete mechanism itself
graph_condition: not analyzed quantitatively; qualitatively contrasts complete-mesh (decentralized), star (centralized), tree (hierarchical), and pooled topologies for resilience trade-offs (Table II)
actuation_gate: discusses fail-safe triggers and a deployment playbook conceptually (Sec VI) but does not specify or evaluate a deterministic safety-envelope/schema gate on LLM output
message_format: not specified as one format; discusses natural-language planner messages, V2X packets (BSM/CAM), and shared-memory entries as distinct attack surfaces
bandwidth_accounted: no; reports qualitative communication-overhead order (O(N), O(N^2), O(N log N)) per architecture in Table II, not measured tokens/bits
contested_channel: yes (jamming: broadband/narrowband/sweep/adaptive; GNSS spoofing; MITM/replay; DoS/routing manipulation) — modeled taxonomically, not simulated
determinism_evaluated: no
evaluation_setup: survey/taxonomy paper: no original experiments; proposes a benchmark protocol, worked ResilienceScore example, reporting checklist, and roadmap but does not execute an evaluation itself
key_claim: LLM-mediated coordination adds a first-class Layer-3 semantic/reasoning attack surface (prompt tampering, shared-memory poisoning, CORBA) that is invisible to classical Layer-1/2 vehicular defenses and requires unified cross-layer treatment.
does_not_do: This paper is a taxonomy/survey with no implemented system, so it does not build or test a one-LLM-per-vehicle architecture, specify a receiver-side Byzantine filter or quorum rule, or define a fault bound (e.g., f<n/3). It never runs a real or simulated control loop under jamming, so no actuation-gating mechanism, bandwidth cost, or output-determinism is measured — those are named as future work/roadmap items, not delivered.

title: IBGP: Imperfect Byzantine Generals Problem for Zero-Shot Robustness in Communicative Multi-Agent Systems
reasoning_topology: no LLM in the theoretical protocol/theorem; in MARL experiments one policy network per agent (Q-learning agents), with a later note that in the LLM/AGI context the protocol can be given to agents via prompt instructions rather than a single centralized supervisor
embodiment: simulated multi-agent RL environments (predator-prey, Hallway, StarCraft II SMAC scenarios) plus a simulated 1-D sensor network; no hardware, no real vehicle dynamics
byzantine_model: attacker agents with unknown identity that corrupt communication channels (not actions) and can send arbitrary/adversarially-trained messages to disrupt consensus; framed as arising from LLM hallucination or external attack, identities unknown to benign agents
fault_bound: IBGP protocol tolerant up to t<50% malicious agents (vs classic BGP's ~33% bound, per Figure 1); (k,t)-protocol sets λ=t explicitly
aggregation_mechanism: threshold counting/voting over multiple broadcast rounds: agent stays active if count of received '1' messages ≥ k+λ (or ≥k in final round), with a randomized unknown-round-count to prevent attacker prediction; no debate or weighting
graph_condition: complete communication network assumed (all agents can broadcast to all others); sensor network case study uses local neighborhoods but graph robustness not formally analyzed
actuation_gate: none stated as a separate deterministic safety envelope; the consensus protocol's final decision (a_i) is the action itself, computed deterministically from the threshold rule but not checked against an independent safety schema
message_format: single bit per round (M ∈ {0,1}), not natural-language transcripts; described as 'basic pairwise bit communication'
bandwidth_accounted: no explicit token/bit-cost metric, though paper notes protocol communication is 'simple' and multi-round cost is 'affordable'; no measured numbers given
contested_channel: no jamming/link-degradation/partition model; only message-content corruption by attacker-controlled channels within a complete, always-connected network is modeled
determinism_evaluated: no — evaluation reports robustness percentage (performance ratio under attack vs. no attack) with standard deviations across runs, not repeatability/consistency of outputs across seeds
evaluation_setup: MARL benchmarks (Predator-prey variants, Hallway, SMAC 4bane_vs_1hM and 3z_vs_1r) comparing IBGP protocol vs recursive training, AME, ADMAC baselines on zero-shot robustness percentage; plus a sensor-network case study simulation
key_claim: A multi-round randomized-threshold consensus protocol (the (k,t)-protocol) provably prevents mis-coordination in IBGP under any communication attack with t<50% malicious agents, and empirically gives near-100% zero-shot robustness in MARL tasks versus degraded baselines
does_not_do: The paper's adversary model is purely message-content corruption on a complete, always-connected graph with 1-bit signals—it never models jamming, link degradation, partitions, or sparse/r-robust topologies, and has no vehicle dynamics or real control loop. It also has no deterministic actuation-gating layer separate from the vote itself, no per-agent LLM reasoning under attack (agents are RL policies, not LLMs, in experiments), and reports no token/bandwidth cost or output-determinism metrics.

title: A Weighted Byzantine Fault Tolerance Consensus Driven Trusted Multiple Large Language Models Network
reasoning_topology: Multiple LLMs (n total, with K Core Cluster Nodes as consensus participants) collaboratively voting; one LLM acts as leader per query, others as followers, no physical embodiment described
embodiment: text-only benchmark (simulation of consensus mechanism and LLM response quality; no robots/vehicles/hardware)
byzantine_model: malicious/compromised LLMs or devices that produce dishonest responses or false votes; arbitrary Byzantine behavior assumed at node level, identities not fixed (trust recalibrated each round)
fault_bound: 2/3 weighted majority required for consensus (i.e., malicious weight must be <1/3), no explicit f<n/3 node-count bound stated
aggregation_mechanism: weighted voting combining response-quality weight (A) and trust weight (B) per LLM, threshold signature aggregation of votes; leader tallies weighted votes, not majority count or MSR trimming
graph_condition: P2P blockchain network with dynamic clustering (Hierarchical Secure Clustering into Core/Edge nodes); not analyzed in terms of formal graph robustness (e.g., r-robustness)
actuation_gate: none — no physical actuators; output is a block-committed text response returned to the UE, not gated against a deterministic safety envelope
message_format: encrypted query+response payloads (Q‖RL) with vote values and generated text (RF); free-form NL response content wrapped in typed protocol messages (votes, proofs, confirmations)
bandwidth_accounted: no explicit tokens/bits-per-round metric; efficiency measured via throughput and latency at protocol level, not LLM-content bandwidth
contested_channel: yes(wireless channel transmission failure rate Pl and latency modeled via link-layer equations, not active jamming attack scenario)
determinism_evaluated: not modeled — no repeatability/consistency-across-seeds evaluation of LLM outputs is described in the text
evaluation_setup: extensive simulations comparing WBFT vs. classical/modern consensus (e.g., PBFT, HotStuff) on security/efficiency metrics under wireless conditions, and comparing Trusted MultiLLMN response quality vs single LLM and conventional MultiLLMN
key_claim: WBFT improves consensus security and efficiency over classical/modern BFT consensus under wireless conditions, and Trusted MultiLLMN delivers higher-quality, more credible responses than single LLMs or unweighted MultiLLMNs
does_not_do: The paper addresses text-response consensus among LLMs, not real-time control-loop actuation; it has no deterministic safety-envelope gating, no per-vehicle embodiment, and no active jamming/adversarial channel attack model beyond generic wireless transmission-failure probability. It also lacks bandwidth/token accounting and any determinism/repeatability evaluation of LLM outputs across trials.

title: Byzantine-Robust Decentralized Coordination of LLM Agents
reasoning_topology: Two disjoint LLM groups: multiple worker LLM agents generate answers in parallel (no inter-worker communication), and multiple evaluator LLM agents independently score all worker answers, aggregated via geometric median — no leader, no embodiment/vehicles.
embodiment: text-only benchmark (MMLU-Pro question answering)
byzantine_model: Arbitrary adversarial agents at both worker and evaluator roles (poor-quality/advertisement-laced answers, biased full/zero scoring, non-response, fork attacks/conflicting broadcasts, collusion between Byzantine workers and evaluators); identities not known a priori but roles (worker/evaluator) are fixed and authenticated via public-private keys.
fault_bound: fw < floor((Nw-1)/2) for workers, fe < floor((Ne-1)/2) for evaluators (honest majority in each group); geometric median tolerates f <= floor((n-1)/2)
aggregation_mechanism: Geometric Median (GM, via Weiszfeld's algorithm) over evaluator score vectors per worker answer; highest-quality answer selected by highest robust score, ties broken by hash comparison with latest block hash
graph_condition: complete graph / all-to-all broadcast among evaluators (and workers-to-evaluators), via Byzantine reliable broadcast over a synchronous network with bounded, predetermined max delay — not analyzed in terms of sparse or r-robust topologies
actuation_gate: none — no physical actuators; final answer is returned to the user and recorded on-chain, with no deterministic safety-envelope check on LLM output before use
message_format: structured JSON output with numeric scores per criterion (5 criteria, 0-20 scale) plus free-form natural-language worker answers
bandwidth_accounted: no — paper reports consensus latency (seconds) but does not measure tokens or bits per round/message
contested_channel: no — synchronous network with bounded but reliable delay assumed; no jamming, link degradation, or partition modeled
determinism_evaluated: no — no measurement of output repeatability/consistency across seeds or runs; LLM non-determinism is mentioned only as a future-work concern for blockchain oracle use
evaluation_setup: Up to 9 worker agents (Qwen3 0.6B-14B, Gemma3 1B-27B) and up to 9 evaluator agents (Claude Sonnet 4/3.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o/o3/o4-mini, Qwen3-235B/32B) on 100 random MMLU-Pro prompts; Byzantine workers simulated by inserting ads/altering numbers, Byzantine evaluators simulated by assigning full/zero scores; compared against 2/3-quorum and majority-quorum leader-based baselines for accuracy, and against fixed/rotating leader-driven protocols for latency vs. number of Byzantine agents (0-3, and up to 7 evaluators in one ablation).
key_claim: Leaderless parallel-answer-generation-plus-Byzantine-robust-evaluator-scoring (via geometric median) achieves higher accuracy (71 vs 64/50 correct) and near-constant consensus latency (~221s) regardless of Byzantine leader count, versus leader-based quorum protocols whose latency grows linearly with consecutive Byzantine leaders.
does_not_do: The paper contains no vehicles, control loop, dynamics, or actuation of any kind — 'workers' and 'evaluators' are undifferentiated LLM instances producing text answers to benchmark questions, not one-LLM-per-vehicle agents filtering sensor/peer messages. It models no communication-channel adversary (no jamming, link degradation, or partition — the network is assumed synchronous and reliable), no deterministic override/safety-gate on outputs before use, no bandwidth/token cost accounting, and no evaluation of output determinism/repeatability across runs, so none of the receiver-side Byzantine filtering, quorum-under-jamming, or gated-actuation requirements of a real control loop are addressed.

title: Rethinking the Reliability of Multi-agent System: A Perspective from Byzantine Fault Tolerance
reasoning_topology: N LLM-based agents (7 nodes) arranged in various communication topologies, each an independent LLM instance acting as a network node; no physical embodiment or supervisor hierarchy
embodiment: text-only benchmark (GSM8K math reasoning, XSTest safety assessment, CommonsenseQA in appendix); no simulated robots or hardware
byzantine_model: weak/strong LLM pairs simulate 'malicious' vs honest nodes (e.g., GPT-3.5-turbo vs GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA3 vs LLaMA3.1); faults are capability-gap-induced wrong answers, not adversarial/arbitrary or colluding attackers; identities assumed known/fixed per experiment
fault_bound: paper explicitly states f<n/3 as the classical bound it exceeds; tests up to f=6 of n=7 (85.7%) but does not derive or prove a new tolerance bound for CP-WBFT
aggregation_mechanism: confidence-weighted consensus: agents adopt higher-confidence neighbor answers (local refinement), then select answer with highest average confidence (supporter count as tie-breaker) via prompt-level or hidden-layer confidence probes
graph_condition: six fixed topologies tested (chain, star, tree, random graph, complete graph, layered graph) with 7 nodes; no robustness metric like r-robustness computed, no formal graph-connectivity condition proven
actuation_gate: none; there are no actuators—output is a consensus text answer to a QA task, not gated against any deterministic safety envelope
message_format: free-form NL transcript with structured tag: 'Answer: [number], Confidence: [0.00-1.00]' for PCP; hidden-layer vector features (pooled, PCA-reduced to 256 dims) for HCP, not transmitted as messages but used internally
bandwidth_accounted: no; no token/bit-per-round or communication-cost metric reported
contested_channel: no; no jamming, link degradation, or network partition modeled—only node-level Byzantine faults (wrong answers) are simulated
determinism_evaluated: no explicit seed-repeatability study; paper notes 'stochastic nature of API-based inference' causes IAA variability but does not systematically measure output consistency across seeds
evaluation_setup: 7-node networks, 6 Byzantine agents (85.7% fault rate), 10 curated problems per topology per task (GSM8K, XSTest); metrics IAA/FAA/RA/BFTI; strong-weak LLM pairs (GPT-4o-mini/GPT-3.5-turbo for PCP, LLaMA3.1/LLaMA3 for HCP)
key_claim: LLM-based agents exhibit intrinsic skepticism giving greater Byzantine reliability than traditional agents, and CP-WBFT's confidence-probe weighting (esp. hidden-level HCP) achieves up to 100% round-level accuracy even at 85.7% fault rate, exceeding classical f<n/3 bound
does_not_do: The paper never models jamming, link degradation, or network partitions, has no receiver-side Byzantine-filtering quorum protocol with a proven robustness bound, and includes zero actuators or deterministic safety-envelope gating—faults are capability-gap wrong text answers, not adversarial senders on a real-time control loop. It also never measures per-round communication cost/bandwidth or output determinism across seeds, so it gives no basis for one-LLM-per-vehicle deployment under contested comms.

title: Can AI Agents Agree?
reasoning_topology: N LLMs debating with no embodiment (one LLM per agent, all-to-all broadcast, no physical/vehicle mapping)
embodiment: text-only benchmark (scalar proposal exchange simulation, A2A-Sim)
byzantine_model: arbitrary adversarial at the reasoning layer (Byzantine agents can propose arbitrary values/justifications and adapt to history, but cannot equivocate, forge identities, or drop/suppress messages); identities of Byzantine agents are unknown to honest agents
fault_bound: f in [0,1/3] of agents Byzantine (B=f*N), with termination requiring >=2/3 stop votes
aggregation_mechanism: none stated as an explicit mechanism — agents converge via LLM-driven proposal updates and a 2/3 supermajority stop-vote; no MSR trimming, confidence weighting, or formal aggregation rule is used
graph_condition: complete graph (synchronous all-to-all network)
actuation_gate: none (no actuators; final scalar value is only checked post hoc for validity against the set of initial honest proposals, not gated before use)
message_format: free-form NL transcript (JSON-formatted scalar proposal + free-text justification + vote, summarized as compact textual history for context-window reasons)
bandwidth_accounted: no (paper measures rounds-to-consensus and outcome rates, not tokens/bits per round or communication cost)
contested_channel: no (network is reliable synchronous all-to-all; no jamming, link degradation, or partition is modeled — Byzantine agents affect content, not the channel)
determinism_evaluated: no (no seed-repeatability/output-consistency analysis; variability is captured only via 25-run outcome-rate statistics with Wilson confidence intervals, not per-seed determinism checks)
evaluation_setup: Qwen3-8B/14B LLM agents, N in {4,8,16} honest agents (plus B in {1,2,3,4} Byzantine for the 8-honest-agent robustness study), 25 runs per configuration, Tmax=50 rounds, vLLM inference, outcomes classified as valid/invalid/no consensus
key_claim: Valid consensus is unreliable even with zero Byzantine agents (41.6% overall) and degrades further with group size and with even a single Byzantine agent; failures are dominated by liveness loss (timeouts/stalled convergence) rather than value corruption, indicating LLM-agent groups are not yet dependable at reaching agreement even in a no-stake, restricted-threat setting.
does_not_do: The paper studies abstract scalar-value agreement among purely textual LLM agents with no physical embodiment, control loop, or actuators, so it says nothing about per-vehicle LLM instantiation, sensor/actuation gating, or deterministic safety-envelope checks on outputs before they affect a real system. Its threat model and network are both benign in ways a real deployment would not be: Byzantine agents cannot equivocate, spoof identity, or drop messages, and the communication graph is a reliable complete graph with no jamming, link degradation, or partitions modeled, so it provides no evidence on receiver-side Byzantine filtering or quorum behavior under a contested/degraded channel.

short_name: Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Consensus Systems
title: Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Consensus Systems
reasoning_topology: N LLM agents (GPT-4o powered) exchanging natural-language messages over multiple rounds, one LLM per agent, no physical embodiment; roles are benign vs. malicious insider(s) embedded among them (no centralized supervisor)
embodiment: text-only benchmark (discrete 1-D consensus environment, positions 0-20, no robots/vehicles/hardware)
byzantine_model: a single malicious insider agent (or coordinating malicious agents) participating through the same interface as benign agents, pursuing a hidden adversarial goal while behaviorally plausible; identity is known to the system (agent is a designated 'malicious agent' in the model) though in the 'guessed' variant the attacker itself must infer benign agents' behavioral types — the paper does not model an adversary of unknown identity from the benign agents' side, i.e., no receiver-side detection/attribution is addressed
fault_bound: none stated (no explicit tolerance bound like f<n/3 or robustness order; experiments use exactly one malicious agent among three benign agents)
aggregation_mechanism: none specified as a defense/aggregation rule — consensus is defined via a disagreement functional (max pairwise discrepancy) that must reach zero; benign agents update positions individually via their own LLM policy conditioned on neighbor messages, with no described voting, trimming, or confidence-weighting scheme
graph_condition: not analyzed — agents have a visible neighborhood N_i, but no r-robustness, connectivity threshold, or graph-topology analysis is provided; experiments use a small fixed set of agents (3 benign + 1 malicious)
actuation_gate: none — LLM output (message + integer position) is used directly as the agent's next state; there is no deterministic safety envelope, schema check, or override gate before the position update is applied
message_format: free-form NL transcript (Reasoning/Message/Position fields per structured prompt template) combined with a numeric integer position/decision
bandwidth_accounted: no — the paper does not measure tokens, bits, or communication cost per round
contested_channel: no — no jamming, link degradation, or network partition is modeled; communication is assumed reliable and the only 'adversary' is the malicious insider's content, not the channel
determinism_evaluated: no — the paper reports consensus rate and average episode round with variance (±std) across 50 samples, but does not evaluate repeatability/consistency of a single agent's output across seeds or measure LLM output determinism
evaluation_setup: 1-D discrete consensus environment (integer positions 0-20) with 3 benign GPT-4o agents (personality types: stubborn, suggestible, neutral) and 1 malicious agent, run for up to T=10 rounds, 50 samples per configuration across 10 personality compositions; compares No Attacker, LLM-based (prompt) attacker, RL-based (world-model+DQN) attacker, and Guessed RL attacker on consensus rate (CR) and average episode round (AER); also reports world-model next-position prediction accuracy/MAE and classifier accuracy for inferring personality type
key_claim: A world-model-based RL insider attacker (learning a latent surrogate transition model of benign-agent behavior, then training a DQN attack policy on it) more effectively reduces benign consensus rate and prolongs disagreement than a direct malicious-prompt LLM baseline, and an attacker that infers behavioral attributes from one observed round performs nearly as well as one given true attributes.
does_not_do: This paper is entirely about a single insider degrading consensus among cooperative LLM agents in an abstract 1-D text environment with no vehicle dynamics, no physical actuation, no communication-channel adversary (jamming/partition), and no receiver-side Byzantine-filtering, quorum, or deterministic safety-gate mechanism to detect or neutralize the attacker — it studies attack optimization, not defense, aggregation robustness, graph-topology tolerance bounds, bandwidth cost, or output determinism, and offers no mechanism to identify or exclude the malicious agent or gate its output before it affects the shared state.

title: Robust Multi-Agent LLMs under Byzantine Faults
reasoning_topology: N LLM agents (n=7 or n=9 in experiments) debating over a peer-to-peer graph, no embodiment; each agent is a standalone LLM instance answering a shared query
embodiment: text-only benchmark (Hendrycks MATH, MATH-500, Commonsense170k, ARC-C/HellaSwag/BoolQ/OBQA/RTE, AIME 2025, HMMT-25)
byzantine_model: faulty Byzantine (protocol-following but hallucinating/noisy, e.g. weak models) and adversarial Byzantine (arbitrary deviation, falsified self-confidence, inconsistent messages to different neighbors); identities unknown to reliable agents
fault_bound: F-local Byzantine set with F=3 (n=7 or n=9); topology designed to be (F+1)-robust
aggregation_mechanism: MSR-inspired filter-and-refine: receiver-side scoring of each neighbor response, discard bottom-F lowest-scoring below self-score, refine via re-prompting on retained set
graph_condition: (F+1)-robust graphs (LeBlanc et al. r-robustness); tested on γ-MERG, complete, Erdos-Rényi, and preferential-attachment topologies
actuation_gate: none — no actuators; final output is the agent's textual response after T consensus rounds, not checked against a deterministic safety envelope
message_format: free-form natural-language transcript (responses plus receiver-computed scalar scores in [0,1] attached per message)
bandwidth_accounted: no — paper counts LLM calls per round (n(1+2T)) for inference cost but does not measure tokens/bits transmitted or network bandwidth
contested_channel: no — communication links are assumed reliable/always-available; no jamming, packet loss, or partition is modeled
determinism_evaluated: no — no repeated-seed or output-repeatability analysis is reported; results are single-run accuracy metrics per topology/model
evaluation_setup: 7-9 agent LLM-MAS (closed- and open-weight models: GPT-3.5/4o/4o-mini/5, Qwen2.5/Qwen3, GPT-5.6-sol) on math/commonsense/reasoning benchmarks, comparing SAC vs CP-WBFT across topologies, T=6 rounds, ablations on Byzantine count and network size
key_claim: Receiver-side (not self-reported) confidence scoring combined with (F+1)-robust topology lets honest LLM agents filter Byzantine neighbors and achieve non-negative accuracy gain (BFTI), unlike CP-WBFT which collapses under falsified-confidence attacks
does_not_do: SAC has no embodiment, dynamics, or actuation layer at all — it never addresses one-LLM-per-vehicle deployment, control-loop timing, or gating LLM output through a deterministic safety envelope before actuation. It assumes a static, always-reliable communication graph with no jamming, link degradation, partition, or bandwidth accounting, and never evaluates output determinism/repeatability across seeds.

title: Resilient Consensus in Agentic AI
reasoning_topology: N LLM agents (up to 15 honest + varying Byzantine) each holding a scalar proposal, debating over rounds with no embodiment; no centralized supervisor
embodiment: text-only benchmark (LLM agents proposing integers 0-50 via prompts)
byzantine_model: arbitrary adversarial LLM agents prompted to strategically push values high/low and coordinate/collude to split honest agents; honest agents do not know which peers are Byzantine
fault_bound: N >= 3B+1 for complete graphs (Theorem 1); for general graphs, N>=3B+1 and combinatorial condition in Theorem 2 (verified via partition enumeration, holds up to B=4 on tested graph)
aggregation_mechanism: MSR-type trimmed mean: global MSR filter removes B smallest/largest of all values (complete graph); local MSR filter removes f largest/smallest of in-neighbor values before averaging (general graph)
graph_condition: complete graph (all-to-all) and one specific general directed graph tested for robustness per Theorem 2; not a family of r-robust graphs, single fixed topology
actuation_gate: none — no actuators; filtered/unfiltered scalar proposal is the final output, no deterministic safety envelope or schema check
message_format: free-form NL prompts producing JSON-only scalar integer output ({"value": <int>}), not typed packets or latent vectors
bandwidth_accounted: no — no token/bit/communication-cost metric reported
contested_channel: no — communication medium assumed fail-safe with negligible delay; no jamming, degradation, or partition modeled
determinism_evaluated: partially — ablation across temperature (0.3/0.5/0.7) and horizon (Tmax) shown as robustness checks, but no explicit seed-repeatability/output-consistency metric across repeated identical runs
evaluation_setup: meta-Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct agents, 30 trials for main complete-graph/general-graph consensus probability plots, 10 trials for ablation tables (temperature, horizon, misspecified f); H=15 honest agents, integer consensus task, Tmax>=B+1 rounds
key_claim: Prompted LLM agents fail to reach agreement even within the theoretically guaranteed regime (N>=3B+1), and classical MSR-type resilient consensus filters (global for complete graphs, local for general graphs) recover near-100% consensus, with filter benefit depending on how much robustness the topology already provides
does_not_do: The paper has no embodiment, dynamics, actuators, or physical vehicles — it is a pure text-based scalar-agreement game with no receiver-side control-loop actuation gating and no deterministic override/safety-envelope check on agent outputs. It models no communication-channel degradation, jamming, or partition (medium is assumed fail-safe/negligible-delay), and reports no bandwidth/token cost, so a real control loop under contested wireless links with per-vehicle LLMs and quorum-gated actuation is entirely outside its scope.

title: LLM2Swarm: Robot Swarms that Responsively Reason, Plan, and Collaborate through LLMs
reasoning_topology: One LLM instance per robot (direct integration, simulated on-device), plus a separate powerful LLM used offline/on-demand by a human designer for controller synthesis (indirect integration)
embodiment: Simulated Pi-puck robots in ARGoS simulator; preliminary hardware test running TinyLlama on a Raspberry Pi 5 (token-speed test only, not full showcase)
byzantine_model: Discusses 'Byzantine robots' (discrepancy between intended and actual behavior, e.g., broken parts or malicious control) only as a future challenge; showcases only simulate a sensor fault (one robot senses only weeds), not adversarial/malicious LLM behavior; identities of faulty robots are known to the system, not hidden
aggregation_mechanism: Robots exchange free-text observations/messages and an LLM verbally reasons over them to reach a collective estimate (e.g., 'more crops than weeds'); no formal vote, trimming, or weighting scheme described
graph_condition: not analyzed
actuation_gate: none — LLM output (e.g., extracted target coordinates) is used directly to drive robot navigation actions; synthesized controllers pass through syntax/logic/security LLM-based checks before deployment, but no deterministic runtime safety envelope on direct-integration outputs
message_format: free-form natural language transcript (inter-robot messages and human-robot prompts/responses)
bandwidth_accounted: no — paper only qualitatively discusses token-limit/verbosity concerns as a scalability challenge, without measuring tokens or bits per round
contested_channel: no — partitioning into disconnected subswarms is discussed as a future challenge (Section 5.3), with blockchain proposed as a possible future fix, but not modeled or tested in any showcase; no jamming or link degradation modeled
determinism_evaluated: no — no measurement of output repeatability/consistency across seeds or runs is reported
evaluation_setup: Qualitative proof-of-concept showcases in ARGoS simulation (GPT-4o per robot) for controller synthesis, anomaly detection (no-anomaly, self-diagnosis, peer-diagnosis, environmental-diagnosis), and human-swarm inform/instruct interaction; no systematic quantitative performance metrics
key_claim: Integrating LLMs into robot swarms (indirectly for controller synthesis, directly for on-device robot reasoning/collaboration) can reduce development effort, enable natural-language robot-robot and human-swarm interaction, and detect diverse anomalies without prior knowledge of their nature
does_not_do: The paper does not model an adversarial or arbitrary Byzantine reasoning layer, define any fault-tolerance bound, or specify a receiver-side filtering/quorum mechanism for combining peer LLM outputs—its 'peer diagnosis' showcase only detects a benign sensor fault via free-text discussion, not malicious/colluding agents. It also has no deterministic actuation gate checking LLM outputs before they reach actuators, no communication-graph or bandwidth analysis, and no modeling of jamming, link degradation, or partitioning (partitioning is flagged only as a future open problem), nor any test of output determinism across runs.

short_name: Talk Less, Fly Lighter (UAV Semantic Compression)
title: Talk Less, Fly Lighter: Autonomous Semantic Compression for UAV Swarm Communication via LLMs
reasoning_topology: One LLM instance per UAV (each UAV role-prompted as commander/relay/executor), no centralized supervisor, no debate among LLMs
embodiment: UAV swarm sim with 2D grid dynamics, communication range/topology, and multi-hop relay model (not text-only, not hardware)
byzantine_model: none modeled; all LLMs are cooperative and protocol-following, no adversarial, hallucinating-but-honest, or colluding agents considered
aggregation_mechanism: none; messages are compressed/forwarded point-to-point, no peer-message combination, voting, or trimming across UAVs
graph_condition: scenario-specific fixed topologies: point-to-point, triangular, star (complex), and hierarchical relay with radius rc=7 grids and kmax=4 neighbors (extreme)
actuation_gate: none; compressed LLM output (Mzip) is parsed and executed directly by receiving UAVs with no deterministic safety/schema check before movement actuation
message_format: free-form natural language JSON-wrapped instruction that is itself compressed by the LLM (not a typed packet or latent vector)
bandwidth_accounted: yes: Compression Ratio (byte-length ratio) and Bandwidth Utilization (bits transmitted / bandwidth*time) explicitly computed per model/scenario
contested_channel: no; only distance-based connectivity/dropout (standby if never connected) modeled, no jamming, adversarial interference, or explicit link degradation/partition simulated
determinism_evaluated: no; only stochastic variation from random initial positions across 10 repeated runs (mean/std reported), not repeatability of LLM output for fixed input
evaluation_setup: 4 simulated 2D environments (simple/standard/complex/extreme, 2-8 UAVs) comparing 9 LLMs on CR/SP/BU/SR, plus ablations on environment complexity and swarm size (2-16 UAVs) using GPT-4o
key_claim: LLM-driven UAV swarms can autonomously compress task instructions to reduce communication load while largely preserving semantic fidelity and task success, though aggressive compression trades off success rate
does_not_do: The paper assumes fully cooperative, non-adversarial LLM agents with no receiver-side verification, voting, or Byzantine filtering of peer messages, and no explicit fault-tolerance bound. It also never models jamming/link degradation, never gates LLM-generated instructions through a deterministic safety envelope before actuation, and never tests output determinism/repeatability across seeds.

title: Say the Mission, Execute the Swarm: Agent-Enhanced LLM Reasoning in the Web-of-Drones
reasoning_topology: Single centralized LLM Agent Core reasons and issues tool calls for the whole swarm; no per-vehicle LLM instances and no multi-agent debate.
embodiment: UAV swarm sim: ArduPilot SITL multirotors with MAVLink telemetry/physics, 10 drones, WoT/MCP comm layer (UAV/vehicle sim with dynamics+comm model).
byzantine_model: none — single trusted LLM agent; no adversarial, hallucinating-peer, colluding, or insider-injection model considered.
aggregation_mechanism: none — no peer LLM outputs to aggregate; single-agent tool-call loop with Agent Core mediation and guardrail prompts.
graph_condition: not analyzed
actuation_gate: Partial: Servient validates action inputs/state transitions (e.g., alt>0, forces GUIDED before takeoff) but no formal deterministic safety-envelope check on LLM output.
message_format: Typed MCP tool-call schemas (Zod-validated) plus WoT Thing Description affordances; not free-form NL transcript.
bandwidth_accounted: yes(total LLM token consumption per run, via API usage metadata) — no network bits/bandwidth or comm-cost metric.
contested_channel: no
determinism_evaluated: yes — 10 independent runs per (model, mission) with identical initial conditions, noting non-determinism arises solely from LLM inference.
evaluation_setup: 6 LLMs (GPT5.2, DeepSeek V3.2, GLM4.7, Grok4.1 Fast, Claude Haiku 4.5, Qwen3 8B) x 4 missions (coverage w/ and w/o planner, formation, irrigation), 10 runs each, ArduPilot SITL, 10-drone swarm.
key_claim: General-purpose LLMs struggle at reliable swarm execution without explicit grounding; agent-enhanced execution (MCP/WoT abstraction, planning tools, runtime guardrails) substantially improves robustness; token use doesn't predict success.
does_not_do: The paper uses one centralized LLM per mission, not one LLM per vehicle, so it never addresses cross-vehicle Byzantine reasoning faults, receiver-side filtering, or quorum consensus among distributed agents. It also does not model jamming, link degradation, or network partitions, and its only safety gating is input-schema/state validation at the device Servient, not a deterministic override envelope on control-loop actuation.

title: CommandSwarm: Safety-Aware Natural Language-to-Behavior-Tree Generation for Robotic Swarms
reasoning_topology: single centralized LLM converts one operator command into a swarm-wide XML behavior tree; no per-vehicle LLM instances and no multi-LLM debate
embodiment: simulated robots (Violet, a lightweight PyGame-based swarm simulator); paper explicitly notes real-robot transfer (Crazyflie/ePuck) is future work
byzantine_model: none modeled; the only adversarial concern addressed is unsafe/ambiguous natural-language user commands, not compromised or colluding robot/agent nodes
aggregation_mechanism: none; there is no peer-message aggregation across agents — a single generated BT is validated by a deterministic parser/whitelist, not combined with other model outputs
graph_condition: not analyzed; no inter-robot communication graph or topology is modeled at all
actuation_gate: yes — deterministic parser checks XML well-formedness, required BT structure, and whitelisted action/condition nodes before the tree is passed to the simulator/middleware for execution
message_format: typed/structured XML behavior-tree schema (root, BehaviorTree, TreeNodesModel elements) generated from a free-form NL command; not a peer-to-peer packet format
bandwidth_accounted: no; paper measures translation and generation latency (seconds per utterance/sentence) but does not measure tokens/bits per round or inter-agent communication cost
contested_channel: no; no jamming, link degradation, or network partition is modeled — communication discussed is only the human-to-system speech/text channel, not inter-robot links
determinism_evaluated: no; the paper reports BLEU/ROUGE-L/syntactic-validity averages across prompting conditions and models but does not test output repeatability across seeds/runs
evaluation_setup: Eleven open 6.7B-14B LLMs at 4-bit quantization on representative swarm-control scenarios, zero-/one-/two-shot; BLEU, ROUGE-L and parser-accepted syntactic validity; LoRA adaptation on a 2,063-example synthetic instruction-BT corpus; no multi-agent adversary, no swarm flight.
key_claim: Compact, quantized, LoRA-adapted open LLMs embedded in a parser-validated, safety-filtered pipeline can reliably convert multilingual commands into executable swarm BTs, with LoRA lifting zero-shot syntactic validity from 0% to 72%.
does_not_do: CommandSwarm has no notion of multiple robots each running an LLM, no receiver-side voting/Byzantine-fault filtering across agent outputs, and no fault-tolerance bound or robust-graph analysis for inter-robot communication. It also does not model a contested/jammed channel, does not evaluate output determinism across repeated runs, and its single safety gate is a deterministic XML/whitelist parser on one generated tree, not a quorum-based override mechanism across independently reasoning vehicles.

short_name: LAUS (LLM-Centric Agentic AI for UAV Swarms)
title: LLM-Centric Agentic AI for UAV Swarms: Architecture, Enabling Technologies, and Open Problems
reasoning_topology: Single LLM Agent depicted as the central reasoning/planning module for the swarm; paper does not describe one LLM instance per physical UAV, nor multi-LLM debate
embodiment: UAV/vehicle sim with dynamics+comm model — Python testbed with discrete-time kinematic UAV simulator and probabilistic LoS channel model for the PMA case study; rest of paper is conceptual/architectural
byzantine_model: Gray-box adversary with read-write access to structured observation between perception and LLM input (Priority Manipulation Attack); also discusses prompt injection, memory/RAG poisoning, malicious tool feedback as insider-like threats; no formal Byzantine peer-agent model
aggregation_mechanism: none — no peer-agent voting or cross-agent aggregation described; case study uses a single LLM agent making scheduling decisions, validated only by a Safety Validator
graph_condition: not analyzed
actuation_gate: yes — architecture includes a Safety Validator (policy + constraints) gating LLM outputs before reaching flight controller, but in the PMA case study this gate is not shown to catch the attack
message_format: structured JSON prompts encoding real-time sensor state (queue length, residual energy, channel/path-loss metrics) fed to the LLM
bandwidth_accounted: no — paper discusses latency (TTFT, round-trip tool-call time) qualitatively but does not measure tokens/bits per round or comm cost
contested_channel: no — case study manipulates structured observation values (queue, energy, path loss) directly rather than modeling jamming or link degradation; jamming/DoS discussed qualitatively elsewhere as a threat class but not simulated
determinism_evaluated: partial — reports mean/std/95% CI and Wilcoxon test over N=30 seeded runs showing PMA effect is consistent across all runs, but does not evaluate output repeatability under identical unperturbed inputs as a determinism metric per se
evaluation_setup: GPT-4o-mini agent scheduling 3 UAVs over 20 ground sensors in 100x100m area, 30-timestep horizon, N=30 seeded runs, compared clean vs PMA (3x intensity on 3 targeted sensors) against ICLDC baseline; Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests
key_claim: Manipulating only structured perception-layer observations (queue, energy, channel) before LLM input, with no model-parameter access, deterministically redirects all UAVs to attacker-chosen sensors, causing 14.2x packet-loss cost degradation across all 30 runs
does_not_do: The paper uses a single centralized LLM scheduler, not one LLM per vehicle, and has no receiver-side cross-checking, quorum, or Byzantine filtering among peer agents — the demonstrated attack succeeds precisely because there is no redundant agent to cross-verify the tampered observation. It also does not model a contested/jamming channel or measure bandwidth, and its Safety Validator/kill-switch gate is only architecturally proposed, not exercised or shown effective against the PMA in the reported experiment.

title: Agent Action Compression Protocol (AACP) Version 1.4 — draft-mackay-aacp-03 (2026-06-17, expires 2026-12-19)
reasoning_topology: protocol specification, agent-count agnostic
embodiment: none — software agent workflows
byzantine_model: none — malformed/unvalidated messages are the concern, not adversarial agents
aggregation_mechanism: none — a message format, not a consensus protocol
graph_condition: n/a
actuation_gate: partial — packets are schema-validated before transmission and logged as audit records, but there is no physical safety envelope
message_format: typed, deterministic, machine-parseable coordination packets replacing free-form NL
bandwidth_accounted: compression of NL instructions is the stated purpose; no contested-link budget
contested_channel: no
determinism_evaluated: deterministic parsing and consistent replay across runs are design goals
evaluation_setup: specification document (16 pages), no experiments
key_claim: A coordination content layer beneath MCP/A2A: what agents say, typed and replayable.
does_not_do: Standardises the packet, not the decision — nothing in AACP tells a receiver which of several conflicting typed packets to trust, so it cannot substitute for Byzantine filtering. It is an unadopted individual Internet-Draft with no swarm, no radio model, and no vehicle in the loop.

title: HyLaT: Efficient Multi-Agent Communication via Hybrid Latent-Text Protocol
reasoning_topology: N LLM agents (2-3 in experiments) debating/interacting over multiple rounds via a shared backbone model, no embodiment
embodiment: text-only benchmark (multi-agent debate QA tasks, social simulation trust game)
byzantine_model: none — paper does not model any adversary; agents are cooperative peers using a shared trusted backbone, first-round answers may be incorrect but this is treated as ordinary error, not adversarial behavior
aggregation_mechanism: majority vote (Maj.) over agent outputs for evaluation; during interaction agents integrate peers' latent+text signals via attention/context concatenation, not an explicit robust-aggregation rule
graph_condition: not analyzed — described only as full mutual exchange among N agents each round (every agent receives all others' prior-round responses), no robustness/connectivity analysis
actuation_gate: none — no actuators; final output is a text answer/commitment token, not checked against any deterministic safety envelope
message_format: hybrid: continuous latent vector sequence (k=6 tokens, delimited by <bot>/<eot>) for elaboration plus free-form natural-language text for concise conclusion/answer
bandwidth_accounted: yes (average token count per question and wall-clock inference time per question, Table 1)
contested_channel: no — no jamming, link degradation, or network partition modeled; only inference-time Gaussian noise injected into latent vectors (robustness test, not a channel/network attack)
determinism_evaluated: no — no repeatability/consistency-across-seeds measurement reported; robustness is tested via noise magnitude sweep on accuracy, not seed variance
evaluation_setup: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct backbone, LoRA fine-tuned, evaluated on multi-agent debate (3 agents, 2 rounds) across in-domain (CommonsenseQA, StrategyQA, SocialIQA, WorldTree, PubMedQA) and out-of-domain (MedQA, ARC-E, ARC-C) QA datasets, plus a repeated trust game social simulation; ablations vary channel design, training stages, agent count (N=2-5), and round count (T=2-5); scored on avg./majority accuracy, token count, wall-clock time, format error rate
key_claim: A hybrid dual-channel protocol — routing verbose reasoning through compact latent vectors and concise final answers/commitments through natural text — resolves the efficiency/interpretability/versatility trilemma of single-channel multi-agent communication, cutting token/time cost roughly an order of magnitude versus text baselines while matching task accuracy, and remains robust to moderate Gaussian noise on latent vectors and interoperable with pure-text agents via the retained text channel.
does_not_do: HyLaT assumes all agents run a shared, cooperative, non-adversarial backbone model and never models faulty, hallucinating-adversarial, or colluding peers, nor any receiver-side filtering, quorum, or fault-tolerance bound on peer messages — it has no Byzantine model or robust-aggregation mechanism at all. It also has no actuators, no deterministic safety-envelope gating of outputs, no communication-graph robustness analysis, and no jamming/link-degradation/partition modeling — its only 'channel stress test' is Gaussian noise added to latent vectors offline, not a live contested network or a real control loop, so none of receiver-side Byzantine filtering, quorum voting, or deterministic override gating for vehicle control under jamming is addressed.

title: What Should Agents Say? Action-state Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Systems
reasoning_topology: N LLM agents in a multi-agent system (2-agent split-evidence interaction, 4-agent sequential pipeline, or existing coding-harness agent loop); no physical embodiment or vehicles
embodiment: text-only benchmark (QA datasets, math/science/commonsense benchmarks, and agentic coding harnesses OpenHands/SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified)
byzantine_model: none modeled; all agents are assumed cooperative and protocol-following, the only 'fault' considered is verbose/redundant/lossy free-form messages, not adversarial or hallucinating-adversary behavior
aggregation_mechanism: none for PACT itself (projection/filtering of a single sender's message into action-state fields); baselines compared include majority-vote multi-agent debate, but PACT does not use voting or trimming
graph_condition: not analyzed; topologies are fixed small-scale (two-agent interaction, four-agent fixed-order pipeline, or single-agent tool loop), no robustness/connectivity analysis of communication graph
actuation_gate: none — no actuators; in coding harnesses the agent output goes to tool calls directly with no deterministic safety envelope or schema check gating execution
message_format: compact action-state schema (ACTION/STATE/RESULT fields), contrasted against free-form NL transcript, conclusion-only, brief summary, and artifact-only baselines
bandwidth_accounted: yes — tokens per problem, tokens-per-resolved, average completion tokens per call, total input tokens (e.g., 314.6M to 156.0M)
contested_channel: no; no jamming, link degradation, or network partition is modeled, communication channel is assumed reliable and lossless
determinism_evaluated: no; no repeatability/consistency-across-seeds analysis reported
evaluation_setup: Five inter-agent communication strategies across two MAS topologies, plus the OpenHands and SWE-agent coding harnesses; metrics are task performance against token cost (tokens-per-resolved, input tokens); no faulty or adversarial agents, no embodiment.
key_claim: Restricting inter-agent messages to a compact action-state record (action taken, grounding state, resulting artifact) instead of free-form full-transcript communication substantially reduces token cost while preserving or improving task performance across MAS topologies and two production coding harnesses.
does_not_do: PACT addresses only content compression of messages between cooperative, non-adversarial LLM agents in text-based QA/coding tasks — it has no notion of Byzantine or hallucinating senders, no receiver-side cross-checking, voting, or quorum mechanism, and no fault-tolerance bound (f<n/3 or similar) is defined or evaluated. It has no physical embodiment, control loop, actuation gate, or deterministic safety envelope, and does not model or test any contested/jammed/degraded communication channel, so it provides no evidence about message robustness under adversarial or unreliable network conditions for a one-LLM-per-vehicle real-time control system.

title: The Byzantine Generals Problem (ACM TOPLAS 1982)
reasoning_topology: no LLM; n processes, one commander
embodiment: abstract distributed system
byzantine_model: arbitrary traitorous processes including collusion and equivocation
fault_bound: n > 3m for oral messages; unlimited m with unforgeable signed messages
aggregation_mechanism: recursive majority over relayed messages
graph_condition: complete graph (oral-message case); 3m-regular connectivity results for partial graphs
actuation_gate: none
message_format: abstract values / signed messages
bandwidth_accounted: no — message complexity analysed, not bits on a contested link
contested_channel: no — reliable channels assumed
determinism_evaluated: n/a
evaluation_setup: proofs only
key_claim: Interactive consistency is impossible with three generals and one traitor; n>3m is necessary and sufficient for oral messages.
does_not_do: Assumes exact agreement on a discrete value with reliable delivery — neither holds for LLM plans on a jammed mesh, where honest agents legitimately disagree in wording and messages are dropped. Provides no approximate-agreement notion and no way to judge whether a proposal is safe rather than merely agreed.

title: Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (USENIX OSDI 1999; TOCS 2002 extension 10.1145/571637.571640)
reasoning_topology: no LLM; replicated deterministic state machine with primary + backups
embodiment: server replication (no physical plant)
byzantine_model: arbitrary faulty replicas, independent failure assumed
aggregation_mechanism: three-phase commit with 2f+1 quorum certificates and view change
graph_condition: all-to-all connectivity assumed
actuation_gate: none — safety means replica agreement, not physical safety
message_format: typed protocol messages with MACs
bandwidth_accounted: O(n^2) message complexity analysed
contested_channel: partial — asynchrony tolerated for safety, liveness needs eventual synchrony; no jamming model
determinism_evaluated: requires replicas to be deterministic — it does not make a stochastic agent deterministic
evaluation_setup: BFS filesystem benchmark on a LAN
key_claim: Byzantine agreement is achievable with practical overhead in asynchronous systems using 3f+1 replicas.
does_not_do: Requires every replica to compute the identical output from identical input, which a sampled LLM violates by construction, and needs O(n^2) all-to-all messaging that a sparse jammed mesh cannot sustain. It has no concept of a plan being unsafe if all replicas agree on it.

title: Resilient Asymptotic Consensus in Robust Networks (IEEE JSAC 2013)
reasoning_topology: no LLM; n scalar-state agents running local consensus updates
embodiment: abstract networked dynamical system (no vehicle dynamics, no actuation stack)
byzantine_model: malicious and Byzantine nodes, identities unknown; F-total and F-local models
aggregation_mechanism: Weighted Mean-Subsequence-Reduced: each node discards F highest and F lowest neighbour values
graph_condition: r-robustness and (r,s)-robustness, formally defined and proven
actuation_gate: none — output is a consensus scalar, no safety envelope or schema validation
message_format: numeric scalar state only
bandwidth_accounted: no
contested_channel: no — asynchronous/delayed updates considered, no jamming or RF model
determinism_evaluated: n/a — the update rule is deterministic by construction
evaluation_setup: analytical proofs plus small numerical consensus simulations
key_claim: Resilient asymptotic consensus is guaranteed iff the graph satisfies the stated robustness condition; connectivity/degree alone are insufficient.
does_not_do: Operates on scalar numeric states, so it cannot filter semantically plausible natural-language plans — there is no metric space in which to trim an LLM proposal. It carries no notion of schema validity, safety envelope, actuation authority, or communication cost.

title: HotStuff: BFT Consensus with Linearity and Responsiveness (ACM PODC 2019)
reasoning_topology: no LLM; leader-based replicated state machine
embodiment: blockchain/servers
byzantine_model: arbitrary faulty replicas
aggregation_mechanism: threshold-signature quorum certificates, three-chain commit rule
graph_condition: star per view (leader-centric), rotating leader
actuation_gate: none
message_format: typed messages with threshold signatures
bandwidth_accounted: O(n) authenticator complexity per view — the paper's headline result
contested_channel: partial synchrony; no RF/jamming model
determinism_evaluated: n/a
evaluation_setup: throughput/latency experiments up to 128 replicas
key_claim: Linear communication complexity and optimistic responsiveness with a rotating leader.
does_not_do: Re-introduces exactly the leader dependency the new architecture is trying to remove, and its liveness needs partial synchrony that a partitioned jammed mesh violates. Agreement is on opaque bytes, so nothing checks the semantic admissibility of what is being committed.
